target: Ecco il libro che cercavi da tempo.
english: Here is the book you've been looking for.
tip: Imperfetto plus da plus a time span means had been doing: cercavi da tempo = you had been looking for a while.

target: Bravo, hai fatto un ottimo lavoro oggi!
english: Well done, you did an excellent job today!
tip: Fare has the irregular past participle fatto, so the passato prossimo is hai fatto, not hai fato.

target: Vieni qui, devo dirti una cosa importante.
english: Come here, I need to tell you something important.
tip: Object pronouns attach to an infinitive, which drops its final -e: dire plus ti becomes dirti.

english: There are many tourists in summer.
tip: Ci sono means 'there are' (plural); c'è means 'there is' (singular). Many tourists takes ci sono: ci sono molti turisti.

english: Look at that beautiful sunset tonight!
tip: bello shortens to bel before a masculine noun: bel tramonto.

target: Ci sono dei fiori nel giardino.
english: There are flowers in the garden.
tip: dei, from di plus i, means some before a masculine plural noun: dei fiori.

target: Il professore è giovane e simpatico.
english: The professor is young and nice.
tip: simpatico means nice or likeable, not sympathetic.

target: Non conoscevo nessuno in quella città.
english: I didn't know anyone in that city.
tip: Italian keeps both negatives: non before the verb plus nessuno after it together mean not anyone: non conoscevo nessuno.

target: Purtroppo il negozio è chiuso il lunedì.
english: Unfortunately the store is closed on Monday.
tip: The article with a weekday means every one of them: il lunedì = on Mondays.

target: Nevicava molto e abbiamo chiuso le scuole.
english: It was snowing a lot and we closed the schools.
tip: Imperfetto sets the background, passato prossimo marks the event: nevicava (was snowing) frames abbiamo chiuso (we closed).
For health and how you feel, use stare, not essere: sto bene = I'm well, literally I stay well.
Italian uses avere (have) where English uses be: ha torto = he's wrong, literally he has wrong.
Fear takes avere, not essere: ha paura = she's afraid, literally she has fear.
Put più before an adjective or adverb to say more: più forte = louder.
Names of languages take the definite article: studi l'italiano = you study Italian.
Bene is the adverb (well); buono is the adjective (good). Canta bene = sings well.
The present tense also covers the near future: parte stasera = he's leaving tonight.
Use stare plus an adjective for a temporary state: sta zitto = he keeps quiet.
Parere means to seem, an everyday match for sembrare: pare contento = he seems happy.
Unlike English, nationalities are written in lowercase: sono italiano = I am Italian.
È with an accent is the verb is; e without it means and: lui è alto = he is tall.
Adjectives ending in -e use one plural, -i, for both genders: felici.
Adjectives ending in -e like triste do not change for gender: a man or a woman is equally triste.
Questions keep statement word order; only the rising tone changes: sei sicuro?
Being right takes avere: avere ragione = to be right, literally to have reason.
To make a verb negative, place non right before it: non ho capito = I didn't understand.
For an informal -are command, drop -re and end in -a: mangia = eat.
Informal commands from -ere and -ire verbs end in -i: chiudi = close.
Being in a hurry uses avere: abbiamo fretta = we're in a hurry, literally we have hurry.
Before a feminine noun starting with a vowel, una drops to un': un'applicazione.
